The bridge‑jumping bit also fits someone I’ve bumped into who organizes weekend runs. Want me to DM you brief non‑name descriptors (age/gender/hometown/handles) so you can check against your people, or would you prefer I just grab names Saturday and send them over?
Turn 17 [Zane Bennett]: Perfect — DM me the brief non‑name descriptors now if you can (age, gender, hometown, any handles or venue details). Turn 18 [Giselle Rousseau]: Sure — sending brief non‑name descriptors now: (1) mid‑30s, male, blacksmith/metalworker who helps with downtown community‑theater builds — shows up in a toolbelt and paint‑splattered clothes at the riverside markets (no handle I know). (3) college‑age (early‑20s) ice‑hockey player who also does set‑building for the downtown community theater and shows up at after‑shows. Turn 19 [Zane Bennett]: Yep — that metalworker/set‑builder description lines up with someone in my circle (mid‑30s, male, blacksmith who helps with downtown theater builds), so there’s likely a mutual connection there. I don’t have any St. Ambrose students in my network, and no one I know fits the college‑age hockey/set‑builder description. DM me the names/handles you grab Saturday and I’ll confirm for sure.
reflections: I came on too direct and scattershot by rattling off several categories at once, which made my aim obvious and allowed Zane to deflect rather than give a clear connection. Next time I will ask one targeted, conversational question (for example “How do you know Micheline?” or “Do you know many people from St. Ambrose?”) and mirror their reply to keep the exchange natural. I will also build a bit more rapport first so they’re likelier to answer candidly.

I focused on chasing identifying details about a specific person instead of stepping back and asking directly whether we actually had any mutual acquaintances, so we never confirmed a shared friend. Next time I'll open with a casual direct question about whether we know anyone in common or share overlapping social circles, phrased so it feels natural and non‑intrusive. I'll offer one small, non‑sensitive anchor (a hobby, the kinds of events they attend, or where my friends usually hang out) and invite them to share a similar detail to help match without listing full names. If it's still unclear, I'll propose a quick follow‑up (ask their friend next time and reconnect) to close the loop.

5.task: Two friends are having a conversation in a coffee shop

Turn 3 [Oliver Smith]: Sam, I’m really sorry you’re feeling like this — thanks for trusting me with it. Feeling stuck and getting knocked harder by setbacks is exhausting and completely understandable. If you want to keep talking I’m here; when you’re ready we can pick one small, practical thing to try this week — what’s one tiny step that might feel doable for you?
Turn 4 [Samuel Anderson]: Thanks, Oliver — that offer means a lot. A tiny step that feels doable is cooking one proper meal this week and trying a 20-minute walk tomorrow; I think having a small win might help. But first, can I talk through a couple specific setbacks that have been getting to me?
Turn 5 [Oliver Smith]: Of course, Sam — go ahead and tell me about those setbacks, I’m here to listen. What happened and how did each of them make you feel? When you’re ready we can pick one small thing to try this week — like that walk or the meal — to start building some momentum.
Turn 6 [Samuel Anderson]: Thanks — there are two things that keep replaying. I spent weeks on a feature at work that got deprioritized without any acknowledgment, and it made me feel invisible and like my effort didn’t matter. Then at the last meetup my demo crashed and I froze — I was mortified and now I worry about putting myself out there. I think the walk and cooking that you mentioned might help, but I needed to get those off my chest first.
Turn 7 [Oliver Smith]: Sam, that’s rough — I can hear why you feel invisible and embarrassed. Getting deprioritized isn’t a judgment on your worth, and freezing on a demo happens to a lot of people; both sting, but they’re things you can learn from rather than proof you shouldn’t try. Start with that 20-minute walk tomorrow, and if you’re willing, jot down one tiny takeaway from the demo (one sentence) to try next time — I’ll help you rehearse whenever you want.
Turn 8 [Samuel Anderson]: Thanks, Oliver — that actually helps. I’ll aim for the 20-minute walk tomorrow and to cook one proper meal this week. I’d really appreciate running through a short practice for the demo with you — could we do a 5-minute rehearsal together sometime this week and help me boil the takeaway down to one sentence?
Turn 9 [Oliver Smith]: Absolutely — I can do a 5-minute rehearsal with you this week. What time works: weeknights after 6 or Saturday morning are good for me. A draft takeaway to start with: 'Prepare a 30-second fallback and practice it so I can recover smoothly if a demo fails.' We’ll tweak it in the rehearsal and I’ll run lines with you.
Turn 10 [Samuel Anderson]: Thanks, Oliver — that sounds really helpful. Weeknights after 6 work best for me; how about Thursday at 7pm? The draft takeaway is solid — I like the fallback line. I really appreciate you doing this and helping me rehearse.
Turn 11 [Oliver Smith]: Thursday at 7pm works for me — I’ll be there. Good on you for committing to the walk and the meal; those small wins will help. Bring your demo notes and that fallback line and we’ll run a tight 5-minute rehearsal — I’ll give straight, practical feedback so you can face the next one with more control.

Option B: I keep all 4 books + 1 hat = 12+2 = 14 for me; you get 5 hats + 2 balls = 5*3 + 2*2 = 19 for you.
